so-say-we-all.$description: So Say We All. So Say We All: a carrier's combat information centre at night, gunmetal and warm low light, with friend and foe on the plot in green and red (Anthony's idea and name, 2026-11-20). Red against green is the hardest pair for red-green colour blindness, so our boat's green is far lighter than the threat's red, and the warning is a hot pink, so the alarms stay distinct (roadmap 223).

yamamoto.$description: Yamamoto. Tokyo Night: deep indigo, soft blue text, pastel signals. Named for the admiral, and for the palette's city (Anthony's call, 2026-11-09). The ground is the palette's darker #16161e, not its #1a1b26, for the faint text and frames' sake, as Polaris and Graveyard Watch do (Anthony's call, 2026-11-13). The caution is paled and the threat deepened a little from the palette's, so colour-blind players can tell them apart (roadmap 223). Charted marks are the palette's teal.

solarpunk.$description: Solarpunk. Solarized (Ethan Schoonover's palette), leaning solar-punk: solar green for nominal, yellow caution, orange threats, red warnings, cyan for your own ship. Labels are base0 and frames base01, so both read on base03 (roadmap 176). The red, the orange and the storm's magenta are Solarized's own, brightened for contrast; so are the yellow, the violet magnetism and the blue velocity (roadmap 223), the yellow far enough that colour-blind players tell it from the orange. Charted marks are base2, Solarized's light paper.

luna.$description: Luna. Luna: deep purple, one hue from a near-black plum ground to pale lilac readings, as Red Light is red and PF3 green (Anthony's idea and name, 2026-11-18). Named for Anthony's dog, Luna: a black coat and a purple collar. The labels are lifted to 6.5:1, so they read without leaving purple. The alarms keep their own hues, a pale yellow, a red and the orange threat, set far enough apart that they stay distinct under each common colour-vision deficiency. Charted marks are the purple at full strength, a vivid violet apart from the paler readings.

via-lactea.$description: Via Lactea. Via Lactea, the Latin for the Milky Way (Ovid, Metamorphoses I); our word galaxy is the Greek for it, galaxias, "milky". The first light theme (Anthony's pick and name, 2026-11-19): a pale verdigris ground, the colour of weathered bronze, with dark bronze readings, after the Antikythera mechanism, a Greek geared device of about 2,000 years ago that predicted eclipses and the planets' places, often called the first known analogue computer. Its instrument colours are flat inks, like a painted atlas of the ancient Mediterranean: Tyrian purple for threats, maroon for warnings, ochre for caution. Our boat is Venetian blue: the Roman fleet's scout boats, says Vegetius (De Re Militari IV.37), had their sails and rigging dyed venetus, sea blue, and their crews wore it, so they could scout unseen by day and night. Roman ghost boats. The alarms are set apart in lightness as well as hue, so they stay distinct under red-green colour blindness. Charted marks are rose madder, a red dye the ancients knew.

sol.$description: Sol. Sol, the Latin for the sun, a pair with Via Lactea (Anthony's idea and name, 2026-11-19): a flat, bright home-computer look of black frames and black readings on yellow. The ground is a soft butter yellow, not a full-strength one, which tires the eyes over a long watch; a cream or soft yellow ground is what the British Dyslexia Association's style guide recommends over white for some readers. Yellow and orange vanish on yellow, so the alarms are dark inks: amber for caution, crimson for warnings and burnt brown for threats, set apart in lightness so they stay distinct under red-green colour blindness. Charted marks are a deep teal, the one dark ink hue left free.

common-ghost-environment.$description: Common Ghost Environment. Common Ghost Environment: the Common Desktop Environment, the Unix desktop of the 1990s on Solaris, HP-UX and AIX, the desktop many people first learned Unix on (Anthony's call and name, 2026-11-19). The ground is CDE's own tan window colour, #c6b2a8, and the frames its slate, #686f82, both from Default.dp in CDE's source (cde/programs/palettes), released under the LGPL in 2012. Motif's raised and sunken bevels cannot be drawn with box characters, so the palette carries the look. On that mid-tone ground every reading must be dark: black readings, a slate label, CDE's teal deepened for our boat, and dark inks for the alarms (umber, wine and navy), apart in hue and lightness for colour-blind eyes. Charted marks are a deep violet ink.

yg-80-garbage-scow.$description: YG-80 (Garbage Scow). The TRS-80 Model I: bluish-white text on black, from a converted black-and-white set. The nickname its owners gave it, as a boat: YG is the navy's hull code for a garbage lighter, and 80 the machine's number, spelled out so the joke lands. Also the insult a famous ship's engineer once threw a punch over (Anthony, 2026-11-14). It had no colour: the alarms borrow some, and charted marks borrow the house colour's rose.

player-missile.$description: Player Missile. Player Missile: the 8-bit home computer whose BASIC screen was one blue, lighter text on a darker ground of the same hue, named for its hardware sprites, "player-missile graphics" (Anthony's call, 2026-11-18). Its chip could show 256 colours, so every colour here is one it could show. The ground is deepened so the readings and alarms read on it; the red is pale for the same reason, as on Workbench.

field-service.$description: Field Service. The blue of an old PC: the sixteen CGA colours, with one exception. On a blue screen, COND BLUE has to be the bright cyan, faint text is its dark cyan (its light blue barely shows), and the light red is lifted a step (#ff6767 for #ff5555) so a warning clears its floor (roadmap 223). Charted marks are its light blue, lifted (#9a9aff for #5555ff) so they read on the blue.

solid-state.$description: Solid State. The home computer whose title screen opened with a band of colour bars, named for its cartridges' label (Anthony's idea and name, 2026-11-18). Its fifteen colours and nothing else, on black as its games ran: its BASIC screen's cyan carries only black text, so cyan is the readings here. Magenta is the threat, as it had no orange. Charted marks are its grey, the one colour left free that reads.

mode-7.$description: Mode 7. The BBC Micro's teletext screen, named for the mode that showed it: its eight colours, all at full strength, on black. Magenta is the threat, as it had no orange. Only the blue is lifted, for the faint text and silent running, since pure blue barely shows on black. Charted marks are the blue lifted further, to a lavender, as teletext had no ninth colour.

breadbin.$description: Breadbin. Breadbin: the home computer's blue screen and light-blue text, its warm palette for the signals (Anthony's idea, 2026-11-09). Its own light blue on that blue is famously faint, so readings and labels are brightened; the original keeps the frames and faint text. The ground is a darker shade of the same blue, #1f1748 for the original #352879, for the faint text and frames' sake (Anthony's call, 2026-11-13; deepened from #241b54 in 0.11.0 so the faint text clears its 3:1 floor, roadmap 223). Caution and threat are set apart so colour-blind players can tell them (roadmap 223). Charted marks are its light grey.

screen-1.$description: Screen 1. Screen 1: the home computer standard whose default screen was white text on dark blue, named for the BASIC command that set its text screen (Anthony's call, 2026-11-18). Its first chips had Solid State's fifteen colours, and on that blue only white reads, so this takes its second generation's 512-colour palette: every colour here is one of those, the blue deepened so the alarms read on it.

locomotive.$description: Locomotive. The Amstrad CPC's bright yellow on deep blue, named for its BASIC. Every colour is one of its twenty-seven. The yellow is the readings, so caution is its bright white, and the threat its orange. Warnings are its pink, since its bright red barely reads on the blue, and faint text its dark cyan, for the same reason (roadmap 223). Charted marks are its pastel yellow, paler than the readings.

jackintosh.$description: Jackintosh. The Atari ST's GEM desktop, named for its owners' nickname: the green desktop and white windows. The green is darkened to a ground, so the signals read on it, with grey window frames and white readings. The alarms are pale, since a red on green is hard to read. Every colour but the ground is one of the 256-colour set's. The ground is deepened past the set's own green (#005f00) so the pale alarms clear their floor (roadmap 223); in 256 colours it shows as that green.

workbench.$description: Workbench. The Amiga's Workbench 1.3: royal blue, white, black and its bright orange. Orange carries the alarms and white the readings; black draws the frames. The blue is deepened from #0055aa so the orange reads on it (to #003c78 in 0.11.0, roadmap 223), and the red is pale for the same reason. Black cannot be the faint text on that blue, so faint text is a blue-grey of ours.

workbench-2.$description: Workbench 2. Workbench 2: the Amiga's Workbench 2.0 (1990), which put 1.3's blue screen away for a light grey ground, black text, white highlights and a medium blue (Anthony's call, 2026-11-19). Its default palette is grey #aaaaaa, black, white and blue #6688bb; the grey is lifted one step, to #bbbbbb, so the alarms clear 4.5:1 on it, and white draws the frames as the highlights did. The blue deepens for labels and threats, and the alarms are dark inks (umber, wine and the blue) set apart in hue and lightness for colour-blind eyes.

boss-key.$description: Boss Key. Boss Key: a plain white ground in the 16-colour palette of a 1990s office desktop (navy, maroon, purple, teal, green, with grey for the faint marks), so a captain on watch at work looks as if she is filling in a spreadsheet (Anthony's idea and name, 2026-11-19). The name nods to the boss key of DOS-era games: one key that hid the game behind a fake work screen. The era's yellow, red and lime cannot be inks on white, so caution is a dark amber, warnings a deepened red and threats purple. A joke theme, but a real one: navy on white suits players who read best that way. Charted marks are the era's olive, deepened to read on white.
